description_full: Daily Journal Corporation publishes newspapers and websites covering in California, Arizona, Utah, and Australia. It operates in two segments, Traditional Business and Journal Technologies. The company publishes 10 newspapers of general circulation, including Los Angeles Daily Journal, San Francisco Daily Journal, Daily Commerce, The Daily Recorder, The Inter-City Express, San Jose Post-Record, Orange County Reporter, Business Journal, The Daily Transcript, and The Record Reporter. It also provides specialized information services; and serves as a newspaper representative for public notice advertising. In addition, the company offers case management software systems and related products, including eCourt, eProsecutor, eDefender, and eSupervision, which are browser-based case processing systems; eFile-it, a browser-based interface that allows attorneys and the public to electronically file documents with the court; and ePay-it, a service primarily for the online payment of traffic citations. Further, it provides its software systems and related products to courts; prosecutor and public defender offices; probation departments; and other justice agencies, including administrative law organizations, city and county governments, and bar associations to manage cases and information electronically, to interface with other justice partners, and to extend electronic services to the public. Daily Journal Corporation was incorporated in 1987 and is based in Los Angeles, California.

financial_summary: Daily Journal Corp. (S.C.) is a small-cap technology business with a $911M market cap on $88M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +18% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at -2% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $13M in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.12×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
Accruals are elevated at +18.0% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 6.9×.
Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 4.5% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
